title: Foraging rock samphire vs marsh samphire: ID and harvest
subtitle: Two species, two habitats, two different preparations
excerpt: Rock samphire grows on cliff faces and rocky shores around the south and west coasts of the UK. Marsh samphire grows in estuaries and salt marshes in different habitats. Both are edible but different in flavour and preparation. Knowing which species you have before eating is essential.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); BSBI species accounts for Crithmum maritimum and Salicornia europaea; John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: Two plants called samphire grow on UK coastlines and are often confused. Rock samphire (Crithmum maritimum) grows on cliff faces, rocky outcrops, and sea walls mainly along the south and west coasts. Marsh samphire (Salicornia europaea) grows in estuaries and salt marshes around most UK coasts. Both are edible but they have different flavours, different habitats, and different preparation requirements. Identify which you have before picking. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
method for each species: match leaf shape, scent or taste, and the specific coastal
foraging zone
. All three must match before picking.
ID features: rock samphire
Habitat: cliff faces, rocky shores, sea walls, mainly south and west coasts of England and Wales, south coast of Ireland. Not in mud or salt marsh.
Leaves: fleshy, segmented, dark blue-green, with a strong aromatic-petrol scent when crushed. The scent is distinctive and hard to confuse.
Flowers (July to August): small, yellow, in flat-topped umbel clusters.
ID features: marsh samphire
Habitat: estuaries, tidal salt marshes, mud flats. Found around most of the UK coast, especially East Anglia and south coast.
Appearance: bright green, jointed, succulent stems without obvious leaves. Sometimes called glasswort. Turns yellow and red in late summer.
Taste: intensely salty, the flavour of the sea. No strong aromatic scent.
Poisonous look-alikes
Rock samphire belongs to the same family as hemlock and hemlock water dropwort, which are both extremely toxic
look-alike plants

. Confirm the coastal cliff habitat and the strong aromatic scent: hemlock and dropwort lack this scent and grow in different habitats. Do not collect rock samphire without being confident in the scent identification.
When and how to harvest

Rock samphire: June through September. Snip the young shoots and leaf tips with scissors; the older stems become tough and fibrous. Avoid picking from the base; leave the plant to regrow. Do not forage on unstable cliff faces.

Marsh samphire: June through August, when the stems are bright green and tender. Snap or snip the upper stems; leave the lower third of the plant. Pick on a falling tide from firm ground. Do not forage in channels or soft mud.
After harvesting

Rock samphire: rinse well. Blanch briefly in unsalted boiling water for one to two minutes; it is already salty from the sea spray. Use as a pungent flavouring in fish dishes, pickled in vinegar, or raw in small amounts. The aromatic flavour is strong; use sparingly.

Marsh samphire: rinse in cold water to remove mud. Steam or blanch for two to three minutes in unsalted water. Eat as a side vegetable, squeezed with lemon, or blanched and tossed through pasta. The salty flavour means no added salt is needed.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage from the coastline for personal use. Some coastal samphire beds are in Marine Protected Areas or on National Nature Reserves with their own rules; check before foraging. Private coastal land requires the landowner's permission.

rows.symptom: Cannot detect the aromatic scent of rock samphire
rows.cause: The plant may not be rock samphire, or the leaf was not crushed firmly
rows.fix: Crush a leaf section firmly and smell immediately. Rock samphire has a distinctive strong aromatic-petrol scent. If absent, do not eat; hemlock relatives grow in similar coastal habitats.

rows.symptom: Marsh samphire is too salty to eat
rows.cause: Not rinsed thoroughly, or the cooking water was salted
rows.fix: Rinse several times in fresh cold water before cooking. Cook in unsalted water. The natural saltiness is a feature; excess salt means insufficient rinsing.
